$comment: The board is a grid of tiles. Each tile has one terrain type, which decides what can be built there, what it costs to cross, what deposits can hide underneath it, and what a discovery roll there can turn up. Every terrain carries a single-letter CODE: it is printed in the bottom corner of every hex on every map overlay, so there is never an argument about what a cell is when the artwork underneath straddles the grid line. The codes key the travel-speed table in travel.json and the discovery tables in discovery.json.

terrains.name: Grassland
terrains.summary: Flat, open, dull and valuable. The default good ground, riverlands included.

terrains.name: Forest
terrains.summary: Carries tree tokens. Fell them for logs; when the last one goes, the tile becomes grassland.

terrains.name: Hills
terrains.summary: Where the ore usually is, and where a mill or vineyard does best.

terrains.name: Mountain
terrains.summary: The richest ground and the most expensive to cross. Rail through a mountain is a statement.

terrains.name: Marsh
terrains.summary: Peat, clay and fresh water for anyone patient enough to live here. B for bog.

terrains.name: Tundra
terrains.summary: Cold and thin. Cold Snap events hit here first and hardest.

terrains.name: Desert
terrains.summary: Sand and salt. Nothing grows without a well, and the discovery table is not your friend.

terrains.name: River
terrains.summary: A watercourse wide enough to be its own hex. Fresh water and fish, a barge lane running inland, and a wall across any road that has not been bridged.

terrains.name: Lake
terrains.summary: Standing fresh water with land all round it. Barges work it, ships never reach it, and every tile on its rim is waterside.

terrains.name: Shallow Water
terrains.summary: Straits, inshore sea and river mouths. Crossable by bridge, navigable by barge.

terrains.name: Deep Water
terrains.summary: Open sea. Ships only, and no bridge will ever cross it. O for ocean.

features.name: Dense Trees
features.summary: 6 tree tokens. Each felling removes one.

features.name: Exposed Stone
features.summary: A quarry may be built here.

features.name: Fishing Ground
features.summary: A dock built on an adjacent land tile may net fish here.

features.name: Game
features.summary: Hunting is allowed on this tile.

features.name: Herbs
features.summary: Arcane herbs may be harvested here.

features.name: Reeds
features.summary: Counts as flax for rope-making, at 1 per 2 hours.

features.name: Sand
features.summary: A sand pit may be built here.

features.name: Salt Flat
features.summary: Salt may be raked with a shovel, 1 per 2 hours, no mine needed.

features.name: Clay Bank
features.summary: A clay pit may be built here.

features.name: Caves
features.summary: Discovery rolls here can reveal a cave mouth. Entering a cave needs a lit torch or lantern - see travel.json and discovery.json.

siting.$comment:
Where the coast went.

Coast was a terrain that meant 'the edge of the water', which quietly made a shore a KIND OF GROUND rather than something a piece of ground happens to be next to. It cost the map twice: a beach in front of a forest had to be drawn as neither forest nor beach, and a town on a lake could not have a dock at all unless the artist painted a ring of sand round the lake first. The edge of the water is a RELATIONSHIP, and it is stated as one here - read off the map the moment somebody asks, printed on no hex, and true of a river bank, a lake rim and a sea shore alike without three terrains to say so.

waterside.name: Waterside
waterside.rule: A land tile with at least one water tile beside it. It is not a terrain, it is never printed on a hex, and no map has to be redrawn to make one.

kinds.$comment: Which water counts, for the thing being sited. A harbour wants the sea; a tannery only wants water.

grants: fresh water without a well, beside a river or a lake
a dock, and the fishing on the water tile it reaches (features fish)
a harbour, beside the sea, and the shipping that comes with it
water power: a mill or a sawmill on a waterside tile takes the bonus its own line names

declaredBy.$comment: Two keys, because there are two things a shore was doing. Both take one of the kinds above, and tools/validate-data.mjs fails the build on a value that is not one of them.
declaredBy.waterside: a REQUIREMENT, on top of whatever ground the thing already needs: the dock and the harbour. Nothing else will do.
declaredBy.orWaterside: an ALTERNATIVE to the terrain list, the way recipes.json site.orTerrain is an alternative to site.building: the sand pit is desert sand OR the sand any water leaves on its bank. Drawing water is a well, a marsh, or fresh water beside you.
declaredBy.note: Coast in a terrain list used to mean both of these at once, and which one it meant depended on the building. That is the whole argument for splitting it.

waterside.checked: tools/validate-map.mjs: a settlement with a harbour has to stand on a tile the sea reaches, and a river or lake hex with no land beside it at all is not a river or a lake. tools/validate-data.mjs: every waterside and orWaterside value is one of the kinds above.

boardSetup.$comment: Setup for a board dealt from a bag of TILES. That board is shelved - see https://github.com/cdomotor-g/game1/issues/18 - and this block is kept rather than removed, because it is still the right answer for a tile set and because tools/validate-map.mjs reads terrainMix and recommendedTiles to report what a DRAWN board actually holds against what the rules assume. Nothing here is a rule about a drawn map: a continent is not a shuffled tile bag, and validate-map reports the gap without ever failing on it.
boardSetup.faceDownAtStart: All tiles beyond each player's starting cluster of 3.
boardSetup.startingCluster: Each player places a town hall on a face-up start tile plus its two neighbours, at least 3 tiles from any other player.
